title: Seven institutions published the 2025 figure on the same day, and got seven different numbers

blocks.text: On 14 January 2026 the groups that keep the global temperature record published their 2025 annual figure together, by arrangement. Copernicus names the coordination explicitly: ECMWF, NASA, NOAA, the UK Met Office, Berkeley Earth and the WMO timed the release of their data. The Japan Meteorological Agency's analysis sits alongside them. Almost every report of it said the same three words, third warmest, and stopped there. The part underneath is more useful, because the seven numbers are not the same number and the reasons they differ are learnable in about five minutes.
WHAT EACH ONE ACTUALLY PUBLISHED

NASA: 2025 was 1.19 C (2.14 F) above the 1951-1980 average in GISTEMP v4. NASA describes 2025 as slightly warmer than 2023 but within the margin of error, so the two are effectively tied; 2024 remains the hottest year since records began in 1880. The analysis uses more than 25,000 meteorological stations plus ship and buoy sea surface instruments and Antarctic research stations. NASA release 26-003, published 2026-01-14.

NOAA NCEI: 2025 was the third-warmest year since global records began in 1850, at 1.17 C (2.11 F) above the 20th-century average, 0.12 C below 2024 and 0.02 C below 2023. The same report gives the same year as 1.34 C (2.41 F) above the 1850-1900 pre-industrial average. Land was second warmest, ocean third. Published 2026-01-14.

Met Office Hadley Centre: 2025 concluded at 1.41 plus or minus 0.09 C above the 1850-1900 average in HadCRUT5, collated with the University of East Anglia and the National Centre for Atmospheric Science. Third warmest, and the third calendar year above 1.4 C. The Met Office gives the 2023-2025 three-year mean as 1.47 C. Published 03:00 UTC, 2026-01-14.

Berkeley Earth: 1.44 plus or minus 0.09 C above 1850-1900, third warmest, about 0.08 C cooler than 2024 and 0.03 C cooler than 2023. Land averaged 2.03 C above the baseline and the ocean surface 1.03 C. Sixteen countries set new national temperature records, against 104 in 2024, and about 770 million people lived in areas that had a locally record-warm year. Published 2026-01-14.

Copernicus C3S: in ERA5, 2025 was 1.47 C above the pre-industrial level and 0.59 C above the 1991-2020 average, third hottest, 0.13 C below 2024's record 1.60 C. Absolute global mean 14.97 C; global sea surface temperature 20.73 C, third warmest. C3S states that the 2023-2025 three-year average exceeded 1.5 C above pre-industrial for the first time. Published 2026-01-14.

Japan Meteorological Agency: the 2025 annual anomaly was +0.48 C above the 1991-2020 average, equivalently +1.03 C above the 20th-century average, the third warmest since 1891, behind 2024 (+0.63 C) and 2023 (+0.54 C). JMA's long-term trend is about +0.79 C per century. Confirmed present on the Tokyo Climate Center page on 2026-08-09.

WMO consolidated: 1.44 plus or minus 0.13 C above the 1850-1900 average, from an analysis of eight datasets. Two of the eight ranked 2025 second warmest in the 176-year record (DCENT and GISTEMP) and six ranked it third (Berkeley Earth, CMST, ERA5, HadCRUT.5.1.0.0, JRA-3Q, NOAAGlobalTemp v6). DCENT and the China Merged Surface Temperature Dataset were factored in for the first time this year. WMO estimates the absolute average global temperature in 2025 at 15.08 C, with a much larger uncertainty of around 0.5 C on the absolute than on the anomaly. The consolidated 2023-2025 mean is 1.48 plus or minus 0.13 C. Published 2026-01-14.
THE SPREAD IS SMALLER THAN THE UNCERTAINTY

Our reading. Line up only the figures quoted against the same 1850-1900 baseline and the disagreement collapses: NOAA 1.34, Met Office 1.41, Berkeley Earth 1.44, WMO consolidated 1.44, ERA5 1.47. Full range 0.13 C. WMO's stated uncertainty on its own consolidated number is plus or minus 0.13 C, a band 0.26 C wide. The institutions therefore agree with each other to within half the width of the error bar any one of them publishes. Six organisations on three continents, with different code, different sea surface products and different ways of filling unobserved regions, land inside their own uncertainty.

Our reading. The largest apparent gap in the set is not between institutions at all, it is between rulers. NOAA published two numbers for the same year in the same report, 1.17 and 1.34, and the 0.17 C between them is pure arithmetic. HadCRUT5's own data file reads +1.048 C for 2025 against its native 1961-1990 baseline while the Met Office headline for the identical series is 1.41 C against 1850-1900, a difference of 0.36 C. GISTEMP's 1.19 C and JMA's +0.48 C are the same planet measured from different starting lines. A figure quoted without its baseline is not a figure.

blocks.caption: GISTEMP v4 annual anomaly against 1951-1980. The 2025 point is 1.19 C, the number in NASA release 26-003. Same planet as the 1.44 C figure, different baseline.

blocks.text: WHAT IS ACTUALLY DIFFERENT BETWEEN THEM

Our reading. Once the baselines are equalised, three things are left that can move a dataset: which sea surface temperature product it uses, how it fills the regions nobody measures (chiefly the Arctic and parts of the Southern Ocean), and whether it is an analysis of observations or a reanalysis. ERA5 is the highest number in the set and is the only reanalysis in it, a weather model rerun with every observation assimilated, which is expected behaviour rather than an error. Beyond that we will not attribute the residual 0.13 C to a specific mechanism from the published headline figures alone, because the reports do not decompose it and we have not done the decomposition ourselves.

The datasets are not independent of one another. NASA's own release states it plainly: the other groups 'use much of the same temperature data in their analyses but employ different methodologies and models, which exhibit the same ongoing warming trend.' NASA release 26-003, 2026-01-14.

The boring reading, and it is a good one. A few hundredths of a degree between datasets is not news. Nothing physical turns on whether 2025 is called second or third: the gap between it and 2023 is 0.02 C in NOAA and 0.03 C in Berkeley Earth, both far inside the error bars, and NASA says so directly by calling the two years effectively tied. Ranking years is a leaderboard habit borrowed from sport. The finding here is the agreement, not the spread, and the sentence that survives all seven analyses is the dull one: 2015 to 2025 are the eleven warmest years in every dataset, and 2025 stayed near the record while La Nina was cooling the Pacific.
A NOTE ON WHICH FILE, BECAUSE IT CAUGHT US

WMO names HadCRUT.5.1.0.0 as the Met Office dataset in its consolidated analysis. On 2026-08-09 both HadCRUT5 versions were being served and both returned HTTP 200 at the same path shape. Version 5.1.0.0 gives 2025 as +1.0480 C against 1961-1990, which is the Met Office's published 1.41 C once rebased to 1850-1900. The superseded version 5.0.2.0 gives +1.1903 C for the same year, with a confidence band roughly three times wider. This project's own hadcrut5-annual series is built from 5.0.2.0.

Our reading. That is why the chart above is GISTEMP and not HadCRUT5. GISTEMP's stored value for 2025 is 1.19, which matches NASA's published figure exactly, so it can carry a claim. Our HadCRUT5 copy has to move to 5.1.0.0 before it is allowed to say anything about 2025. The general lesson is one this project already writes down and just paid for again: HTTP 200 is not proof of currency. A dead file and a live file look identical from the outside.

The practical takeaway is small and portable. When you see a global temperature figure, ask two questions before you compare it to anything: against what baseline, and from which version of which dataset. Almost all the disagreement you will ever see in coverage of this subject is answered by those two questions, and what remains after them is a genuine, published, well-behaved uncertainty of about a tenth of a degree.

knowledge: The seven 2025 annual figures collected side by side with their baselines attached, and the spread measured: 0.13 C across the five pre-industrial-referenced numbers, against a published uncertainty band 0.26 C wide. Plus a checked defect in our own data path: hadcrut5-annual is built from the superseded HadCRUT.5.0.2.0, whose 2025 value (+1.1903 C vs 1961-1990) does not reconcile with the Met Office headline, while 5.1.0.0 (+1.0480 C) does.
